content: Hand hygiene materials can be implemented in a cost-effective manner by ensuring their optimal placement to align with the workflow and behavior of healthcare workers. To minimize resource demands, it is recommended that lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) prioritize the local production of hand hygiene products as part of their implementation strategies. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) has expressed confidence in the feasibility of this recommendation, emphasizing that it can be achieved through low-cost solutions. Additionally, the GDG believes that key stakeholders will find this recommendation acceptable, as hand hygiene is a fundamental clinical practice for all healthcare workers. Based on the available evidence, which primarily focuses on hand hygiene, the GDG concluded that ensuring the availability and proper placement of hand hygiene materials and equipment at the point of care will significantly enhance the performance of appropriate hand hygiene practices. The GDG also identified research gaps, particularly the need for high-quality studies to evaluate the impact of system changes on reducing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and antimicrobial resistance (AMR), as well as changes in clinical practices. Further investigation into the local production of alcohol-based hand rubs, including aspects of quality control and acceptance, is also necessary. Adoption of these guidelines across all levels of the health system is essential. Success depends on the integration of infection prevention and control (IPC) core components into national action plans for AMR, which aligns with the strategic objectives of the AMR Global Action Plan adopted by all WHO Member States in 2015. The implementation of these guidelines requires a robust strategy and a defined process for adaptation and integration into regional, national, and facility-level strategies. The effectiveness of implementation will depend on the existing health systems, available resources, and policies in each country. Support from key stakeholders, partner agencies, and organizations is critical for success. The WHO IPC Global Unit is collaborating with international experts and stakeholders to develop a resource dedicated to implementation strategies for these guidelines, particularly in resource-limited settings. This includes the creation of new IPC training packages aligned with the core components and best practices. The dissemination of the guidelines will occur through various mechanisms, including online and print formats, WHO web pages, and global campaigns such as Save Lives: Clean Your Hands. Social media and mobile health technologies will also be explored as supplementary dissemination tools. Printed versions of the guidelines will be available in all official United Nations languages, with third-party translations encouraged for additional languages. Technical support for adapting and implementing the guidelines will be provided upon request by ministries of health or WHO regional and country offices. The IPC teams at all levels of WHO will work with stakeholders to identify priorities, barriers, and facilitators for successful implementation. Pilot implementations are planned in selected countries, particularly in the African Region and the Region of the Americas. The guidelines will be reviewed and updated every 3–5 years, informed by lessons learned from previous dissemination and implementation efforts. Mechanisms will be developed to track the adoption of IPC core components in national programs, the number of printed copies and downloads, and requests for technical assistance. These activities will be supported by specific communication strategies and the development of implementation tools.
